I remain skeptical about the potential of RSI. No matter how sophisticated an LLM and its tooling get, there are limits to domain knowledge that an LLM cannot expand with information it does not have. We've seen in math for instance the explosion of discoveries when the LLM was trained on the highly specific domain knowledge of mathematicians and drew reasonable conclusions from that information. But now that information has been exhausted; what further exponential progress can be made, once it has "used up" that knowledge? It needs more guidance to continue forward. So certainly the speed of research will be enhanced, but the idea that we will roll into a self-sustaining dynamo of discovery seems thermodynamically impossible. There are also physical limitations. Suppose with the domain knowledge of quantum physicists and fusion engineers, an LLM is able to solve two of the hardest applied physics problems: the mass qubit alignment problem, and fusion reactors that reliably produce net energy. There will nonetheless be lag time before a sophisticated quantum computer and fusion reactor will be built, and mass production will take years. This is assuming these problems can be solved at all, or if we will discover unfortunately that we are limited by the laws of physics and there are simply no scalable solutions for these technologies. We just don't know.
